title: The DNA double helix is published

when.label: 25 April 1953
when.note: Date of publication of Watson and Crick's paper in Nature.

where.name: Old Cavendish Laboratory, Free School Lane, Cambridge
where.note: The Cavendish Laboratory was then on Free School Lane; it has since moved to west Cambridge.

summary: James Watson and Francis Crick, working at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in a short paper in Nature.
description: On 25 April 1953 the journal Nature published 'Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid' by J. D. Watson and F. H. C. Crick, proposing that DNA is made of two helical chains.

Their model drew on experimental data from several researchers, including Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London. In 1952 Franklin had used X-ray diffraction to capture 'Photo 51', which revealed DNA's helical shape.
context: Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids.

facts.text: Watson and Crick's paper was published in Nature on 25 April 1953.
Crick, Watson and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

uncertain.text: Franklin's role has long been debated. In a 2023 Nature article, historians Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort argued from newly examined 1953 documents that she was 'an equal player' rather than a victim whose data were simply taken.
